en.title: Food and drink
en.goal: Order food and drink at a restaurant and express simple preferences.
vocab: a cup of tea (杯 in context)

phrases.t: I'd like a cup of tea.

dialogue.title: At the restaurant
lines: Hello, what would you like to eat?
Okay. Would you like some coffee?
No, thank you. I like drinking tea.

hen-adjective.title: 很 (hěn) before an adjective
hen-adjective.body: In Chinese, simple sentences with an adjective almost always put 很 (hěn) before it — even when you don't mean "very". Without 很, the sentence sounds like an implied comparison or is grammatically odd.

yao-xihuan.title: 要 (yào) — "to want"
yao-xihuan.body: 要 (yào) expresses want or need, both before a noun ("I want tea") and before a verb ("I want to go"). It is one of the most common words in everyday Chinese, especially for ordering.
examples: I'd like a cup of tea

yao-xihuan.title: "Xǐhuan" or "yào"?
yao-xihuan.body: Xǐhuan (喜欢) means to like something in general, a preference — it is followed directly by what you like (a noun or another verb). Yào (要) means to want something specific, right now. One talks about taste, the other about a request.
examples: I'd like a cup of tea (right now)

cha-origem-china.title: China is the birthplace of tea
cha-origem-china.body: Tea comes from China — it has been drunk there for thousands of years, and the very word "tea"/"chá" in many languages comes from Chinese words (chá 茶, depending on the trade route). Serving tea to guests is an important part of Chinese hospitality to this day.

trueFalse.claim: This phrase is used to order something at a restaurant or café.
trueFalse.whyNote: Correct — 我要...(wǒ yào) means "I want", used to order something at a restaurant or café; here, "a cup of tea".

review.why: 'delicious' or 'good (to eat)' also fit; 好吃 is literally 'good to eat'
